newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thai, Cambodia crisis may spur change in ASEAN.
newsitem.headline: Thai, Cambodia crisis may spur change in ASEAN.

text.p: Thailand's financial woes and Cambodia's political crisis could spur the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) to greater economic deregulation and regional cooperation, a consultancy report said on Monday.
The Hong Kong-based Political Risk Consultancy (PERC) said it was extremely significant that the downward pressure on most ASEAN currencies was taking place at the same time as the Cambodian crisis.
It said Thailand's problems and Cambodia's crisis had created pressure for change in the way the organisation did things.

"This could be by coordinating policies better and developing certain regulatory standards on a regional basis, or it could mean isolating countries that pursue irresponsible policies," the report said.
Asia needed to improve its financial sector infrastructure, including the banking industry of various countries, stock markets and their regulatory structure, PERC said.

It said most governments were having to abandon rigid foreign exchange rate management policies because of a Thai crisis which has seen the baht drop more than 20 percent against the dollar over the last month.
Other currencies, notably Malaysia's ringgit, have dropped by lesser amounts, but this did not mean a long period of competitive devaluations, PERC added.
Hong Kong's institutions had come through in the best shape, underscoring its suitability as a regional trading and financial centre despite the transition to Chinese sovereignty.
"Hong Kong's political status may have changed but not its economic institutions...better able to withstand the shocks of a Thai-style crisis than the other economies of the region."
Overall, PERC said that Southeast Asia would not suffer an outflow of capital from Thailand's financial troubles.
Instead, the crisis was likely to lead to smarter flows.

"The Asian region will still be growing economically at a much faster rate than any other region of the world, and the higher rates of interest that will result from the Thai fallout will help to attract capital, not scare it away," PERC said.
It said currency speculators may be correct to regard Indonesia as vulnerable, as its institutional structure was not much stronger than Thailand's.
But the governments of Malaysia, Singapore and Philippines had not allowed imbalances to develop in their economies nearly to the extent of the Thai government, it added.

PERC said ASEAN's decision not to admit Cambodia last month as planned after second prime minister Hun Sen ousted first prime minister Norodom Sihanouk in two days of fighting, marked a redefinition of the group's philosophy.

"Instead of respecting Cambodia's right to become even more politically messed up than it is already, ASEAN is now trying to lead an effort to help restore a more stable form of government," the report said.
It said the Cambodia decision meant ASEAN, which has always reached decisions by consensus, had put aside a policy of non-interference in the internal affairs of others.
The organisation would now have to develop a new system for discussing issues and reaching compromise solutions that fall short of consensus, it said.
